8.1.b:
A good total knee arthroplasty (TKA) starts in the clinic, so the chapter opens with the patient, not the saw.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you assess a patient before TKA?"
- "Ask about **previous surgery**, old trauma, injections and drugs: each one changes a decision."
- "Examine alignment, joint line, ligaments, skin, vessels, and always the **hip and spine**."
- "Labs include **urine**, ECG and echo; a raised CRP or ESR means **synovial biopsy** first."

### History
The history decides more outcomes than the instruments do.

#### Indication
- TKA treats **pain** that persists after failed conservative care
- Never decide on the X-ray alone: an Ahlbäck grade 4 film is not an indication by itself

#### Patient Selection
- A never-satisfied patient usually reflects **poor selection**, not poor skill (Prof Abdel Karim)
- So study the patient first, then the knee
[[FIG: Fig 8.1 · 8.1
- Under **50**, TKA is wrong, except in inflammatory arthritis
- Over **90**, decide on function: does the patient walk, live alone, drive?

#### Previous Surgery and Trauma
- **Previous surgery** (arthroscopy, osteotomy) leaves scars that dictate the approach
- An old deformity needs releases, and bone loss needs augments
- Old trauma matters too, so always ask about it

#### Injections and Drugs
- Ask about any previous **knee injection** (hyaluronic acid, steroid); it is almost never asked
- An injection raises the risk of infection
- **Anticoagulants** stop 1 week before, bridged with subcutaneous Clexane (enoxaparin)

#### Body Build
- Estimate **weight and thigh size**; a female leg gives a false impression of thigh size
- A male **manual worker** with big muscle bulk obstructs the subvastus view, so it shapes the approach

### Examination
The examination maps the deformity and the soft tissues that will hold the implant.

#### The Knee
- **Alignment**: varus or valgus, and any fixed flexion deformity (FFD) or recurvatum
- The **joint line** level shows bone loss and where it comes from
- The **ligaments** decide how much constraint the prosthesis needs

#### Skin and Vessels
- Look for excoriations, cellulitis and ulcers
- Check the **vascular** status for ischaemia
- **Varicose veins** mean more bleeding and a harder dissection

#### Infection and Remote Causes of Pain
- An active skin infection or open **ulcer** postpones elective TKA until it heals
- Clear any **remote infection** first, such as dental or urinary
- Always examine the **hip and spine**: hip arthritis refers pain to the knee via the obturator nerve

MEMORY HOOK — the obturator gossip
- The obturator nerve is a gossip: it carries the hip's complaints down to the knee, so examine the hip.

### Investigations and Optimisation
Tests then confirm that the patient is fit and the knee is clean.

#### Laboratory Tests
- Labs include **PT and PTT** (prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times), ECG and echocardiography
- **Urine analysis** is often omitted, yet UTI (urinary tract infection) is common
- An untreated UTI causes post-operative problems

PITFALL — raised CRP and ESR before a "simple" TKA
- Case: CRP (C-reactive protein) 10, ESR 60–80; **synovial biopsy** and culture showed TB synovitis (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Say → "**rheumatology referral and synovial biopsy before TKA**, or the knee turns septic after surgery"

#### Optimisation
- Screen for super-obesity, diabetes, hypertension and a previous **DVT** (deep vein thrombosis) in that leg
- After open-heart surgery, postpone TKA for at least **1 year**
- After coronary **stents**, wait 6 months (Prof Sherif Khaled)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Pain, not film · scars · injections · anticoagulants · urine · hip and spine · CRP up = biopsy**

8.2.b:
With the patient ready, films show the deformity and let you size the implant before the first cut.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which films and why?"
- "**Standing AP, lateral and skyline** films, plus a **long-leg standing film** (scanogram)."
- "The long film shows the **mechanical axis**, extra-articular deformity, and whether an IM guide can pass."
- "Template after calibrating **20%** magnification: axes, cuts, then femoral and tibial **size**."

### Standard Radiographs
Every TKA needs the same basic set, and some knees need more.

#### Knee Films
- Order **standing AP** (anteroposterior), **lateral** and **skyline** (Merchant) views of the knee (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 8.2 · 8.2

#### Long-Leg Standing Film
- The **scanogram** is a long-leg standing AP with the patella forward
- It is mandatory before every TKA, routine in Europe but rarely done locally
[[FIG: Fig 8.3 · 8.2
- It is a must with deformity, or with height ≤152 cm or >190 cm

#### Deformity and Hardware
- The long film rules out **extra-articular deformity**: femoral bow, old fracture, tibial bowing
- Deformity or **retained hardware** blocks IM (intramedullary) guides
- So use EM (extramedullary) or navigated guides instead
[[FIG: Fig 8.4 · 8.2

#### Computed Tomography
- Without a standing long film, as often in Egypt, order a **CT scanogram**
[[FIG: Fig 8.5 · 8.2
- CT of the distal femur shows the TEA (transepicondylar axis), for rotation
- **3D CT** is not routine: complex primaries with a suspected defect, mainly revision
- In revision, 3D CT shows **defect size**, loosening and fracture extent, despite metal artefact

### Interpretation of Each View
Each view answers one question for the plan.

#### AP and Weight-Bearing Views
- The AP shows the affected compartments (**medial, lateral, PF** = patellofemoral), deformity and defects
- Subluxation means bone loss or instability, so plan a **constrained** prosthesis
- A **weight-bearing** view shows coronal laxity; unprepared laxity leaves residual instability
[[FIG: Fig 8.6 · 8.2

#### Lateral and Flexion Views
- The **lateral** is taken in extension and flexion; a long cassette helps sizing
- A missed **posterior osteophyte** tightens the flexion gap, so it must be removed
- The **Rosenberg view** (weight-bearing PA in flexion) shows posterior-compartment narrowing

#### Stress and Axial Views
- **Stress** films show whether the deformity corrects and the convex-side collateral is competent
- The **axial** view shows patellar dysplasia and trochlear hypoplasia, so PF maltracking is avoided

### Templating
Templating turns the films into a plan, so theatre holds no surprises.

#### Aims and Payoff
- Plan alignment in 3 planes, implant size, augments for defects, and any hypoplasia
- It shortens the operation and adds precision, more so as cases get harder
- An **extreme size** the company did not bring causes trouble in theatre

#### Steps and Calibration
- Check the films and their **magnification** first
- Then analyse axes, angles and cuts, and template the femur, then the tibia
- Magnification is ≈**20%**: a knee-level 10 mm marker reads 12 mm, even on digital films
[[FIG: Fig 8.7 · 8.2

MEMORY HOOK — the flattering X-ray
- The X-ray flatters every knee by 20%: the 10 mm marker poses as 12 mm, so calibrate before you believe.

#### Joint Centres
- Femoral head: **Mose circles**, or bisect the head diameter
- Knee: notch apex or condylar midpoint; tibia: between the **spines**
- Ankle: the **talar dome** centre
[[FIG: Fig 8.8 · 8.2

#### Angles and Femoral Fit
- The **hip–knee–ankle angle** (femoral vs tibial mechanical axis) gives the coronal deformity
[[FIG: Fig 8.9 · 8.2
- Femoral AP: perpendicular to the mechanical axis, both condyles covered; **overhang** is worse than undersize
- Femoral lateral: maximum coverage, with no flexion or extension of the component

#### Tibial Fit and Accuracy
- Tibia: perpendicular to its mechanical axis on AP, parallel to the **anterior cortex** on lateral
- Against navigation, templating is accurate for femur on **lateral** 83%, tibia on **AP** 80% (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Within ±1 size, accuracy rises to 100% and 93%

#### Stems and Software
- Mild femoral extra-articular deformity takes a **short rod**; a large one, osteotomy plus stem
- The osteotomy and the TKA go together or staged
- Revision stems: plan the size, as it is often unavailable
[[FIG: Fig 8.10 · 8.2
- Primary stems: varus >15°, obesity, osteoporosis (debated)
[[FIG: Fig 8.11 · 8.2
- Case: NexGen tibial stem **15 × 75 mm**, 120 mm with the keel, under an LPS-Flex 10 mm insert
- The PFC Sigma short tibial stem (60 × 13 mm) is always **cemented**
- Software replaces acetate: **OrthoSize**, OrthoView, TraumaCAD

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Standing AP + lateral + skyline + long film · 20% · femur on lateral, tibia on AP**

8.3.b:
Before cutting, fix the targets, because every later cut serves these goals.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are the goals of TKA?"
- "**Mechanical axis** neutral, **joint line** restored, **balanced** equal rectangular gaps."
- "Correct component **rotation** and good **patellofemoral tracking**; balancing is the key step."
- "Numbers: **6-3-7** = distal femoral valgus 6°, femoral external rotation (ER) 3°, slope 7°."

### The Six Goals
Six goals define a well-done TKA, and they lean on each other.

#### The Goals
- Neutral **mechanical axis**, restored **joint line** and ligament balance
[[FIG: Fig 8.12 · 8.3
- Equal symmetrical gaps, correct component **rotation** and PF tracking
- Axis, joint line and balance are one goal seen three ways; a miss in one is not rescued

#### Balancing and Tracking
- TKA is a **soft-tissue balancing** operation, so balancing is the most important step
- Measured resection, gap balancing and alignment philosophies → 09 Balancing
- **PF tracking** is often forgotten, especially without resurfacing

#### The 6-3-7 Rule
- **6°** distal femoral valgus, **3°** femoral ER, **7°** posterior tibial slope (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Each number varies; say "**distal femoral valgus angle**", never just "valgus angle"

MEMORY HOOK — dial 6-3-7
- Dial 6-3-7 to reach a good knee: valgus 6, rotation 3, slope 7. Every patient, though, has a slightly different number.

### Mechanical Axis
The mechanical axis is the first goal and the easiest to measure.

#### Definition
- It runs from the femoral head centre to the **talar dome** centre on the long film
- It lies at **3° ± 1.5°** to the vertical
- Through the knee centre it is neutral; medial is **varus**, lateral is valgus

#### Femoral and Tibial Axes
- The femoral **anatomical axis** bisects the shaft at two levels ≈10 cm apart
- It lies **6°** from the mechanical axis and ≈9° from the vertical (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- That angle between the two femoral axes is the **distal femoral valgus angle**
- The tibial mechanical axis runs from the proximal tibial centre to the ankle centre

#### Native Joint Orientation
- The native tibial surface sits at **87°** (≈3° varus), and the femur at 93°
- So the native joint line is parallel to the ground

#### Malalignment
- An error ≤**3°** is acceptable, but still aim for neutral (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Beyond 3°, outcome and survivorship fall
- Malalignment brings **wear**, aseptic loosening, tibiofemoral and PF instability, patellar fracture, stiffness

### Joint Line
The joint line is the second goal, and it sets the height of the patella.

#### Landmarks
- It lies **10 mm** below the lower pole of the patella and 30 mm below the medial epicondyle
[[FIG: Fig 8.13 · 8.3
- It lies 25 mm below the lateral epicondyle and 10–15 mm above the **fibular head**
- Campbell gives 28 mm (medial), 23 mm (lateral) and 14 mm (fibula)
- In revision, peripheral **meniscal remnants** mark the native line, but they are rarely found
- Joint-line landmarks on films → 10 TKA radiographs

#### Raised or Lowered Line
- A **raised** line gives patella baja
- A **lowered** line (tibial over-cut, thin insert, short distal cut) gives alta, incomplete extension, flexion instability
- An excess distal cut with a thick insert raises it: **pseudo-baja**, mid-flexion instability, anterior knee pain

PITFALL — how far may the joint line move?
- Prof Sherif Khaled allows up to **8 mm**, beyond which comes baja; Campbell says avoid elevation >**4 mm**
- Say → "**keep it within 4 mm**; more costs motion, patellar function and mid-flexion stability"

#### Joint Line and Implant Design
- **CR** (cruciate-retaining) knees tolerate little joint-line change
- **PS** (posterior-stabilised) knees accept mild elevation (Campbell)

### Patellofemoral Tracking
The last goal is a patella that runs in its groove, and component position decides it.

#### Q Angle
- The **Q angle** lies between ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine) to patellar centre, and patellar centre to tuberosity
- Normal is **13–18°**, larger in females (≈18°)
- Campbell calls >15° in men and >20° in women abnormal
- Q-angle drawing and maltracking → 16 Knee problems

#### Component Position
- The rule: **lateralise everything except the patella**
- The femoral component goes lateral, and lateral again between sizes; never medialise it
- The tibial tray is lateralised too
- The button sits medial, central or superior, never inferior
[[FIG: Fig 8.14 · 8.3
- **Never internally rotate** the femoral or tibial component
- IR moves the tuberosity laterally, so the Q angle rises and the patella subluxes laterally

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **6-3-7 · axis ≤3° · line ≤4 mm · up = baja · lateralise all but the patella · never IR**

8.4.b:
With the targets set, the knee must be opened: the medial parapatellar route is the workhorse, and the others answer special cases.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "describe your approach"
- "Supine, tourniquet, **midline incision** in flexion, **medial parapatellar** arthrotomy with a quadriceps **cuff**."
- "It suits primary, complex primary and revision knees, and **all deformities**."
- "**Subvastus** for easy primaries, **lateral** for valgus >15°, **extensile** for stiff or revision knees."

### Choice of Approach
The choice rests first on training and familiarity, then on scars, deformity, stiffness and revision.
- Medial parapatellar, midvastus and subvastus show **no outcome difference** (Campbell)

### Positioning and Preparation
A good set-up saves an assistant and lets you check alignment later.

#### Set-up
- The patient lies **supine**, with an ECG lead over the femoral head centre to check the rod
[[FIG: Fig 8.15 · 8.4
- A bolster and foot rest hold the knee, so no assistant is needed
- The tourniquet is padded and high; exsanguinate with an Esmarch

#### Tourniquet
- Inflate with the knee **flexed**, so the quadriceps is longer and tracking is true
- Tourniquet use is debated; Prof Sherif Khaled lately operates without one
- A very obese ("shawarma") thigh is done without one
- Some inflate only for cementing, which needs a sterile tourniquet

#### Skin Preparation and Antibiotics
- **Shave on the table** only; earlier shaving leaves small wounds that get infected
- At induction give **ceftazidime** (Fortum) 1 g and **tranexamic acid** 1 g IV, before inflation
[[FIG: Fig 8.16 · 8.4
- A compression bandage leaves the foot palpable, so the **2nd metatarsal** can guide tibial rotation

### Medial Parapatellar Approach
This is the approach to describe in the exam, step by step.

#### Skin Incision
- Mark the incision and raise **thick flaps**, because undermining causes skin slough
[[FIG: Fig 8.17 · 8.4
- Make it midline with the **knee flexed**, which keeps it shorter
- It runs from 5 cm above the patella to 1 cm below the tuberosity

#### Previous Scars and Nerve
- An old **transverse scar** is crossed safely by a longitudinal incision at 90°
- With **multiple scars**, use the most lateral usable one: skin blood comes from medial (Campbell)
- The incision cuts the **infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve**, so warn about lateral numbness and neuroma

#### Arthrotomy
- Cut along the **quadriceps tendon**, leaving a 3–4 mm cuff on vastus medialis (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 8.18 · 8.4
- Continue round the medial patellar border, then 3–4 cm onto the anteromedial tibia beside the **patellar tendon**
- Leave 1 cm of tendon and 1 cm of cuff for **extensor closure**
- The proximal limb is ≈8 cm: less in thin patients, barely enough in obese

#### Medial Release and Variants
- Elevate the capsule and **deep MCL** (medial collateral ligament) subperiosteally to the posteromedial corner
[[FIG: Fig 8.19 · 8.4
- With the knee extended and the patella everted, release the lateral **PF plicae**
- Lift one medial sleeve to the midline, 5–8 cm down; no more release at this stage (Prof Shokry)
- The **Insall** variation cuts over the patella; closure is hard (transosseous sutures), so it is unpopular
[[FIG: Fig 8.20 · 8.4
- It leaves no soft tissue on the patella, which suits planned **resurfacing**

#### Patellar Eversion

### Tibial Cut
The tibia is cut perpendicular to the mechanical axis, whatever the deformity.

#### Tibial Axes
- The anatomical and mechanical axes normally coincide
- They do not after a childhood malunion or **congenital bowing**
- So the "tibial cut angle" is **0°**, unless the tibia is deformed
- Components in >5° varus subside into more varus: **medial overload**, early loosening (Campbell)

#### Extramedullary versus Intramedullary Guide
- The **EM** guide runs from knee centre to ankle centre; it sees the ankle, so bowing cannot mislead
- No canal is opened, so there is less **fat embolism**, and deformity is bypassed
[[FIG: Fig 8.29 · 8.5
- The **IM** guide follows the anatomical axis: neutral in 83% of varus but 37% of valgus knees (Campbell)
- Within 2° of 90°, IM vs EM scored **94% vs 85%**, or 72% vs 88%; Campbell uses EM

#### Setting the Rod
- Aim the rod over the **medial ⅓ / lateral ⅔** of the tuberosity
- Distally it points to the ankle centre, toward the **2nd metatarsal** (or 2nd–3rd space)
- The foot alone is unreliable, so draw the **tibial crest** and the 2nd metatarsal line
[[FIG: Fig 8.30 · 8.5
- The crest is absent 10–15 cm above the ankle
- Keep the ankle at **90°**: a turned or plantarflexed foot changes the reference
- Mark **tibialis anterior** before the drape, or palpate it in dorsiflexion
- Set the **level** first, then **rotation** along the crest

- Say → "**slightly medial to the intermalleolar midpoint**, because the medial malleolus is more prominent"

- Hohmanns sublux the tibia forward; one placed toward the **MCL** protects it
- Put the **lateral pins first**, because the sclerotic medial condyle deflects pins
[[FIG: Fig 8.31 · 8.5
- An angel wing previews the cut
- Place a **protector** between patellar tendon and saw, and check both ends of the piece
- Remove the bone semi-flexed, with meniscal and **PCL** (posterior cruciate ligament) remnants and posterior debris

### Posterior Tibial Slope
Seen from the side, the tibial cut tilts backward, and that tilt opens only the flexion gap.

#### Native and Designed Slope
- Jigs build in **0°, 3° or 7°** of posterior slope
[[FIG: Fig 8.32 · 8.5
- Native slope is **7–10°**; reproduce the manufacturer's slope, near the patient's own
- Companies differ: DePuy 3° or 5°, **Zimmer 7°**; many build 3° into the insert
- Slope opens the **flexion gap only**; depth opens both gaps

- Slope is a hinge at the back door: it opens only the flexion gap, while depth lowers the whole floor.

| Slope error | Result |
|---|---|
| **Excess** (>7–10°) | wide flexion gap, limited extension, FFD · PCL insertion cut |
| PS + excess | post impinges anteriorly · flexion instability |
| **Reversed** (anterior) | limited flexion, recurvatum · sinking on weak anterior bone |

#### Matching Slope to the Implant
- An implant without built-in slope, with none cut, gives an **inverted slope** in every patient
[[FIG: Fig 8.33 · 8.5
- On the template, native 5° means a 5° jig; native 3° never means 7° or 10°
- A PS insert has slope built in, so cut 0°; in **CR** knees, cut the slope into bone
- An insert thicker in front than behind has slope built in
- Equal thickness front and back means the slope must be cut into bone

- The proximal 10–15 cm of tibia is enough, so no long lateral film is needed

[[FIG: Fig 8.34 · 8.5

How deep to cut depends on the less worn side, never on the defect.

#### Depth

- The stylus reads 8, 9 or 10 mm, depending on the company

- An excess cut lowers the joint line and loosens the extension gap
- It also leaves smaller components on weak cancellous bone
- Kept tibial bone also makes a later **revision** easier

- A stylus on the defect gives a **very large** cut, so reference the normal side
- Defect **<5 mm** → cement; contained → impacted cancellous graft (Campbell)
- Larger uncontained → structural graft, metal wedge (augment), or screws in cement

8.6.b:
The distal cut fixed the extension gap; femoral rotation and size now shape the flexion gap, and the patella comes last.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you set femoral rotation?"
- "Parallel to the **TEA**, perpendicular to **Whiteside's line**, or **3° ER** to the posterior condyles."
- "No axis is 100%, so **mark all three** and cross-check; gap balancing adds a fourth."
- "Patella: cut medial more than lateral, total **20–23 mm**, residual ≥12–13 mm."

### Femoral Rotation
Rotation decides whether the flexion gap is rectangular, so it gets three references and a cross-check.

#### Why 3° External Rotation
- The native tibia has **3° varus**, so the medial condyle projects more posteriorly in flexion
[[FIG: Fig 8.43 · 8.6
- A 90° tibial cut with the femur parallel to the PCA (posterior condylar axis) leaves a **trapezoidal** gap
- 3° ER makes it rectangular and equal to the extension gap
- A medially worn tibia cut at 90° loses ≈2 mm medially versus 9–10 mm laterally

#### Reference Axes

| Axis | Definition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Surgical TEA** | epicondylar prominences | most used · ≈3° ER to PCA |
| **Whiteside's line** | deepest trochlea to notch centre | ≈91° to TEA, range 80–102° |
| **PCA** | posterior condyles | rotate 3° ER |

- The anatomical TEA is not seen in surgery, so it is ignored
[[FIG: Fig 8.44 · 8.6
- Whiteside's line alone can err by up to **10°**
- **Marking is mandatory**, before the cuts and before the entry point
- Use a posterior referencing jig (NexGen **0 and 3**), with an anterior stylus ≈2 cm above the trochlea
[[FIG: Fig 8.45 · 8.6

#### Deformity and the Posterior Condylar Axis
- **Valgus** and rheumatoid knees have a hypoplastic lateral condyle
[[FIG: Fig 8.46 · 8.6
- The PCA is then off by up to **10°**, so 3° ER still leaves ≈7° of internal rotation (IR)
- So J&J jigs offer 3°, 5° or 7° of ER
- In valgus, use anterior referencing and cut posteriorly **parallel to the TEA**

| Valgus deformity | Femoral ER (Prof Abdel Karim) |
|---|---|
| standard | 3° |
| 10–20° | 5° |
| >20° | 7° |

- In **varus**, the PCA is already externally rotated, so 3° may be unneeded
- ER is tolerated better than IR

#### Cross-checks
- A fourth reference: cut the **tibia first**, then set the femur parallel after balancing extension
[[FIG: Fig 8.47 · 8.6
- **Grand piano sign**: the lateral peak of the anterior cut ≈2× the medial means correct rotation
[[FIG: Fig 8.48 · 8.6
- Rotation errors causing maltracking → 16 Knee problems
- Component rotation on CT → 10 TKA radiographs

MEMORY HOOK — the grand piano
- Rotation is right when the anterior cut plays a grand piano: the lateral key stands twice as tall as the medial.

### Femoral Sizing
With rotation set, the size decides the flexion gap and the fit at the front.

#### Sizing Systems
- NexGen is sized by **AP** diameter; later came ML (mediolateral) sizes and a gender knee
[[FIG: Fig 8.49 · 8.6
- Size steps were 6–8 mm, now **2 mm**, so the margin of error is smaller
- PFC Sigma has half sizes (2, 2.5, 3); between sizes choose the larger, since you can downsize
- The sizer's anterior foot sits where anterior cartilage meets cortex, on the **highest lateral** point
- Clear the suprapatellar synovium off the anterior femur first
- Size changes show **posteriorly**; the distal thickness stays 9–10 mm (Handbook)

#### Size Errors
- Remove femoral **osteophytes** before sizing, to read the true ML size
- Undersizing risks fracture on impaction and instability
- Oversizing brings overhang pain, less flexion, maltracking and higher PF forces
- An undersized tibia **subsides** on impaction

PITFALL — anterior or posterior referencing?
- **Anterior**: no notching, but the flexion gap varies between sizes; **posterior**: gap kept, but notching or overstuffing (Campbell)
- Say → "**know which system you use**; it decides the gap when you change size"

#### Posterior Condylar Offset
- It runs from the posterior femoral cortex tangent to the back of the condyle
- The **offset** removed must be replaced
[[FIG: Fig 8.50 · 8.6
- Less offset (posterior over-cut, small femur) → **limited flexion**, poly impingement, faster wear
- Offset figures → 07 Knee design

### Finishing Cuts
The four-in-one block then makes the remaining femoral cuts in a fixed order.

#### Checks Before Cutting
- An **angel wing** confirms that the anterior cut will not notch
- Posterior resection is 8–9 mm, medial more than lateral
- **Lateralise** the block for tracking, and put the medial pins first
- Notching or a wrong resection means a wrong **entry point**; remove pins before the chamfers

#### Order and Box Cut
- Order: anterior, posterior, anterior chamfer, posterior chamfer; protect the tibia and MCL
- Zimmer cuts anterior, anterior chamfer, posterior, posterior chamfer; Prof Shokry says order matters little
- The **notch** block is for PCL-sacrificing designs only (the cam seat); CR knees keep the bone
[[FIG: Fig 8.51 · 8.6
- Bone from the anterior chamfer plugs the canal, so it bleeds less
- Box cut: saw medial, then lateral, then central with a **narrow** blade; the block leaves the cam seat
- Keep the bone bridge between the condyles: an empty middle breaks
[[FIG: Fig 8.52 · 8.6
- Score the patellar-track lines, cut the trochlear recess, then smooth it with an osteotome and file

- A **curved osteotome** clears posterior osteophytes and meniscal and PCL remnants
- Mind the **neurovascular bundle** behind the capsule

#### Notching
- About to notch? Stop, finish the other cuts, then step down deliberately
- If notched, use a **stemmed** femoral component
[[FIG: Fig 8.53 · 8.6
- Notching and supracondylar fracture → 15 Periprosthetic fractures

### Patellar Cut
The patella is the optional last cut, and first you decide whether to resurface it at all.

#### Resurfacing Debate

| Resurfacing | Points |
|---|---|
| For | less **anterior knee pain**, better PF function |
| Against | fracture, AVN (avascular necrosis), loosening · 5–60% |

- Excise excess fat pad and synovium

- Measure thickness before surgery on the **Merchant view**; plan by the bone you keep

[[FIG: Fig 8.54 · 8.6

- Measure with **calipers** before and after the cut, and drill with a **stopper**
- Without a stopper the 3-peg drill **perforates** a thin patella, and it fractures

- Under 12–13 mm of residual bone, do not resurface
- Clamp the patella so the saw cut is straight

- Over-resection brings fracture; under-resection overstuffs: pain, tilt, limited flexion
- Say → "**restore the original thickness**, measured before and after the cut"

- Button position → 16 Knee problems · patellar fracture → 15 Periprosthetic fractures

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Inflammatory = resurface · medial more · 20–23 total, ≥12 left · button medial**

### Trial Reduction
Trials test every earlier decision while changes are still free.

#### Trials
- Clean up, finish the **meniscectomy**, then insert trials with a thin insert and reduce
[[FIG: Fig 8.55 · 8.7
- Re-cut or release now, because after cementing it is a revision
- Balance at 90° and **45°**: sagittal for the gaps, coronal by varus–valgus stress → 09 Balancing

MEMORY HOOK — the dress rehearsal
- The trial is the dress rehearsal: a mistake now costs a re-cut; after cement, the same mistake costs a revision.

#### Femoral Trial
- Check size and side, seat it by hand, and clear blocking bone before hammering
[[FIG: Fig 8.56 · 8.7
- Hammering over an incongruity fractures the **lateral condyle**
- A posterior Hohmann drifting laterally does the same; keep it central, never lever osteoporotic bone

#### Tracking and Insert Size
- Tracking tests, tourniquet deflation and lateral release → 16 Knee problems
- Insert size as a balance check → 09 Balancing

### Tibial Tray Rotation
The tray's rotation decides tracking and comfort, so three landmarks are used together.

#### Landmarks
- Neutral: the tray on the **medial ⅓ / lateral ⅔** of the tuberosity, as in Miller
[[FIG: Fig 8.57 · 8.7
- Campbell uses the medial border instead (Prof Abdel Karim)
- The **2nd ray** fails in foot deformity and rheumatoid knees; aim just lateral to tibialis anterior
[[FIG: Fig 8.58 · 8.7
- **Curve on curve**: the tray's anterior curve sits on the curve of the lateral plateau
- Posteromedial uncoverage of a symmetric tray only confirms rotation; never use it alone
- The **Akagi line** gives slight malrotation, so use the modified Akagi (medial ⅓ / lateral ⅔)
[[FIG: Fig 8.59 · 8.7
- Other lines: transverse axis, widest plateau diameter, PCL insertion, tibial posterior condyles (fully subluxed only)

#### Use Three Together
- Combine curve on curve, the tuberosity third, and the EM rod on the crest to the 2nd metatarsal
- When uncertain, go **1 mm lateral**; place the tray's lateral side and lateral pins first
- Never internally rotate the tray; neutral or slightly external is safe
- Posteromedial uncoverage figure → 07 Knee design

#### Overhang and Keel
- **Medial overhang** irritates the MCL and hurts; excess ER does the same
[[FIG: Fig 8.60 · 8.7
- Tibial overhang is unacceptable (tenting, **arthrofibrosis**); femoral ML overhang gives collateral pain
- Drill the keel in **reverse** to compact osteoporotic bone, then punch
- Mobile-bearing rotation mismatch → 07 Knee design

### Cementing
Cement fixes every decision in place, so order and a dry field matter.

#### Technique
- Use **pulsatile lavage** and dry bone; cement the component undersurface, not the posterior condyles
[[FIG: Fig 8.61 · 8.7
- Cement the **tibia first**, because the femur first crowds the field
- The tibia needs >110° of flexion, especially in obese patients
- On the tibia, cement the base and **proximal keel** only; with pins out, cover the canal

#### Avoiding Errors
- Cement left in the notch hits the post and causes **early loosening**
- Hold a trial insert of the **same** size in full extension until the cement sets
- Gauze under the posterior Hohmann keeps cement off the back of the components
- The final insert goes in tilted posteriorly, then clicks home

#### Cement Type and Tourniquet
- Plain cement is usual, but many prefer **antibiotic-loaded** cement
- Release the tourniquet **after** cementing, gradually: bleeding spoils adherence

- Image intensifier at every step, but none after final implantation (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Say → "**check a film after final implantation**, not only during the cuts"

- Case: a tibial stem exited through a **tibial plateau fracture**
[[FIG: Fig 8.62 · 8.7
- It was revised the next day and followed to 1 year

### Haemostasis, Analgesia and Closure
The last steps limit bleeding and pain, and set up early flexion.

#### Tranexamic Acid and Cocktail
- **Tranexamic acid** 1 g intra-articular plus a periarticular cocktail gives better pain control
- The cocktail: bupivacaine (Marcaine), lidocaine, **ketorolac** and dexamethasone 8 mg
- Inject 1 g into the posterior capsule and gutters; leave 1 g in the irrigation ≈2 min, then suction
- Inject the posterior capsule medially and laterally, **never midline** (neurovascular bundle)
- Infiltration stays in the tissue, so the drain does not remove it; never inject into the drain
- Analgesia is pre-emptive and multimodal

#### Drains
- Most use no drain; Prof Shokry drains all, because bleeding stiffens the knee
- With tranexamic acid ×3 his drain gives 300–400 mL, versus up to 1 L without it
- The drain comes out at 48 h
- Both drains exit **proximally**, so leakage does not alarm the walking patient
- Campbell: routine drains are gone, with no difference in infection or haematoma

#### Closure
- An IM plug cuts blood loss by 20–25% (Campbell)
- Close in **flexion** ≈70–90°, so flexion starts on day one
[[FIG: Fig 8.63 · 8.7
- Close the skin at ≈40° of flexion
